    name = path.split("node_modules/")[-1]    # handles nested and @scope/name
    found = query(name, meta["version"])
    flag = "!!" if found else "ok"
    print(f"{flag} {name}@{meta['version']}")
    for v in found:
        print("     ", v["id"], v.get("summary", "")[:55])

scenes.caption: Load the lockfile. Our test file lists three packages: ua-parser-js 0.7.29, event-stream 3.3.6 and ms 2.1.3.
Skip the empty key, which is the project itself.
First package: POST its name and version to api.osv.dev. One advisory comes back: GitHub's malware advisory for the hijacked release.
scenes.output:
!! ua-parser-js@0.7.29
      GHSA-pjwm-rvh2-c87w Embedded malware in ua-parser-js

scenes.caption: event-stream 3.3.6 matches the advisory shared with flatmap-stream from 2018.
scenes.output:
!! ua-parser-js@0.7.29
      GHSA-pjwm-rvh2-c87w Embedded malware in ua-parser-js
!! event-stream@3.3.6
      GHSA-mh6f-8j2x-4483 Critical severity vulnerability that affects event-stre

scenes.caption: ms 2.1.3 has no known advisories. 'ok' means 'nothing known yet', never 'safe'.
scenes.output:
!! ua-parser-js@0.7.29
      GHSA-pjwm-rvh2-c87w Embedded malware in ua-parser-js
!! event-stream@3.3.6
      GHSA-mh6f-8j2x-4483 Critical severity vulnerability that affects event-stre
ok ms@2.1.3

blocks.caption: Runnable with Python 3 and no extra packages: `python3 osv_lock.py package-lock.json`. Output above is from a real run in November 2026; advisory lists only grow.

blocks.md:
**Two very different findings.** Most advisories describe **vulnerabilities**: honest bugs with a fixed version to upgrade to. **Malware** advisories are different: GitHub notes they have no fixed version, because the defining property is that there are no safe versions of the malicious release, and the response is removal plus incident response, not an upgrade.

**Noise is the real problem.** At the time of writing, OSV returns more than 30 advisories for axios 1.14.0, almost all bugs in specific features, alongside the single `MAL-` entry for 1.14.1. Teams prioritise by: malware first; then whether the vulnerable code is reachable from yours; then known exploitation (CISA's KEV, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, catalogue).

**Project health** is a separate signal. OpenSSF Scorecard grades repositories on checks such as Maintained, Pinned-Dependencies, Token-Permissions and Dangerous-Workflow, which flag risky practices before anything goes wrong.

Scan in two places: in CI on every change (block new malware and serious vulnerabilities from entering) and continuously against what is already deployed, because a package that was clean yesterday can get an advisory today.

blocks.question: Dependabot opens no pull request for a malware alert on a package you use. Why?
options: Malware advisories have no fixed version to upgrade to; the safe action is to remove or replace the package and investigate
Dependabot ignores npm packages
The alert is a false positive
Malware alerts require a paid plan
blocks.explain: GitHub's docs: malware alerts do not contain a fix version, because there are no safe versions of the malicious package. You remove it and treat affected machines as compromised.

blocks.question: The scanner prints 'ok' for every package. What can you conclude?
options: The project contains no malicious or vulnerable code
All dependencies are signed
The lockfile is up to date
No advisory currently matches those exact versions in the databases queried
blocks.explain: Scanners know only what has been reported. Every malicious package in this course was 'ok' for some time after publication, which is why cooldowns and the other layers exist.

lessons.title: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering

blocks.md:
The xz backdoor (CVE-2024-3094, disclosed 29 March 2024) is the most studied open source supply chain attack, and if you took the linux-for-security course you saw how it reached the SSH server; the next lesson recaps that path. These two lessons go deeper: first the human campaign, then how the payload hid and how it was caught.

XZ Utils is a compression library and tool (liblzma is its library). Lasse Collin designed the .xz format with help from others in 2005 to 2008 and maintained the project, in their own words an unpaid hobby project. It ships in almost every Linux distribution. Russ Cox reconstructed the timeline from mailing lists and git history ([Cox](https://research.swtch.com/xz-timeline)); the dates below come from it.

blocks.title: From first patch to disclosure (months since October 2021)

scenes.caption: 29 Oct 2021: a contributor using the name Jia Tan sends a first, harmless patch. More good patches follow; in Feb 2022 Lasse Collin merges their first commit.
Apr to Jun 2022: new accounts, 'Jigar Kumar' and 'Dennis Ens', complain that patches stall and urge a new maintainer. They never appear elsewhere on the internet.
Lasse Collin replies that Jia Tan is practically a co-maintainer already. By Dec 2022 Jia Tan merges commits directly; Lasse's last release is Jan 2023.
2023: Jia Tan makes releases (from March) and redirects oss-fuzz reports to themselves. In June 'Hans Jansen' contributes an ifunc change that later gives the backdoor its hook.
Feb to Mar 2024: payload hidden in test files, backdoored releases 5.6.0 and 5.6.1, pressure on distributions to adopt them. Andres Freund discloses on 29 March.

blocks.md:
The campaign worked on the weak point of open source: maintainers. Lasse Collin wrote to the list in June 2022 that their ability to care had been limited by long-term mental health issues, and that this was an unpaid hobby project. The pressure emails used that. Cox notes that Brian Krebs, a security journalist, found the complaining addresses never appeared elsewhere online, not even in data breaches, which suggests sock puppets (fake personas run by the same operator).

Look at what each step bought: patches built reputation; pressure turned reputation into commit access; commit access gave releases, control of the project website (moved to GitHub Pages in January 2024) and of the fuzzing configuration (fuzzing feeds programs random, malformed inputs to find crashes). In 2024 the same personas returned, asking Debian and Ubuntu to upgrade quickly to 5.6.1. Dominic Tarr had said the same thing about event-stream in 2018: they gave access to someone who emailed asking to maintain it, because maintaining it brought them nothing.

blocks.code:
# Signals you can actually check for a dependency's project health
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/contributors --jq '.[].login' | head   # one person?
git log --since=2.years --format='%an' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
git log --format='%h %an %s' -- tests/files | head             # who adds opaque binaries?

# OpenSSF Scorecard: maintenance, branch protection, pinned deps, dangerous workflows
scorecard --repo=github.com/OWNER/REPO
blocks.caption: None of these would have named Jia Tan as malicious. They show bus factor (how many people the project depends on), new people gaining release rights, and opaque binary files entering the tree, which are where reviewers should look harder.

blocks.md: The xz attack was a trust attack, not a technical exploit of git, signing or builds. Every step was done by a legitimate maintainer with legitimate rights. Defences are partly social: fund and share maintenance of critical projects, add second reviewers for releases, and treat sudden pressure to hand over control or upgrade fast as a warning sign.

blocks.question: Why did the 'Jigar Kumar' and 'Dennis Ens' emails matter to the attack?
options: They contained malicious patches
They pressured an overworked maintainer to hand more control to Jia Tan
They reported bugs that Jia Tan then fixed
They hacked Lasse Collin's account
blocks.explain: They wrote complaints about slow progress and urged a new maintainer. Shortly after, Lasse Collin described Jia Tan as practically a co-maintainer and gave commit access.

blocks.question: Which control would most directly have stopped Jia Tan from shipping 5.6.0 alone?
options: Signing release tarballs
Running unit tests in CI
Requiring a second maintainer to review and approve every release and the release archive contents
Using SHA-256 instead of CRC in xz
blocks.explain: The releases were signed and tests passed. A second, independent person checking that the release archive matched the reviewed git tree is the control aimed at a single trusted insider, which SLSA's Source track formalises as required review.

lessons.title: xz-utils II: where the payload hid and how it was caught

blocks.md: The technical design was as careful as the social one. Andres Freund, a PostgreSQL developer and engineer at Microsoft, described it in the disclosure ([oss-security](https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2024/03/29/4)):

1. **Payload in the repository, disguised as test data.** Two binary files, `tests/files/bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz` and `tests/files/good-large_compressed.lzma`, were committed in February 2024. Compression libraries legitimately keep hand-made corrupt files for testing, and, as Russ Cox's timeline notes, the directory's README already said many were created by hand with a hex editor. Freund notes they were not even used by any test in 5.6.0.
2. **The trigger only in the release tarballs.** The archives Jia Tan built and signed contained a modified `build-to-host.m4` (a macro file for the m4 text processor used by Autotools, the GNU tools that generate the `configure` script a source tarball ships). That line was not in git, and release tarballs routinely contain generated build files that git does not, so it did not stand out.
3. **Narrow conditions.** The injected script ran only when building on x86-64 Linux, with gcc and the GNU linker, inside a Debian or RPM package build. Freund thought the last condition was likely aimed at making the issue harder for investigators to reproduce.

blocks.title: From an innocent-looking test file to code inside sshd

nodes.label:
configure in a
deb or rpm build

scenes.caption: Git holds the source and two opaque test files. A reviewer of the repository sees nothing executable.
The release tarball adds a modified build-to-host.m4. A distribution's package build runs configure, which runs it.
If the conditions match, the script decodes a shell script out of one test file, which extracts a compiled object from the other and links it into liblzma.
On Debian, Fedora and others, sshd (the SSH server) is patched to notify systemd (the service manager), so it loads libsystemd, which loads liblzma. The hidden code now runs inside sshd as root.
At start-up, using a glibc audit hook and the ifunc feature, it redirects sshd's RSA_public_decrypt to its own code before that table becomes read-only.

blocks.md:
The hook point, **ifunc** (GNU indirect function: a way to pick an implementation, such as a fast CRC routine for the current CPU, while the program is being loaded), came from the 2023 'Hans Jansen' patch. It runs code early enough to modify sshd's function-pointer table before it is remapped read-only. Freund traced the redirect of `RSA_public_decrypt`, called during public-key authentication, and concluded the code ran before authentication. Cox's summary of later analysis: it watches for hidden commands from the attacker at the start of an SSH session, giving the attacker unauthenticated, targeted remote code execution.

**How it was caught.** Freund noticed odd symptoms on Debian unstable (sid) systems: SSH logins using a lot of CPU, and errors from valgrind (a memory-error checker). Investigating a half-second slowdown is what exposed it.

blocks.title: Andres Freund's measurement: a failed SSH login, before and after

scenes.caption: Before the update, a login attempt with a nonexistent user took 0.299 seconds of wall-clock time.
With the backdoored liblzma installed: 0.807 seconds. Freund traced the extra time to the code parsing symbol tables in memory, the step that first drew attention.

blocks.md:
Timing mattered. Cox's timeline shows defenders were already closing in by accident: valgrind errors in Red Hat distributions on 4 March; a systemd change, merged 5 March, to stop linking liblzma into libsystemd, which would have broken the attack path; and Jia Tan's 5.6.1 on 9 March, which 'fixed' the valgrind errors by updating the test files. Freund privately notified Debian and the distros list on 28 March; Debian rolled back with a package named 5.6.1+really5.4.5, and Red Hat announced that Fedora Rawhide and the Fedora 40 beta had shipped the backdoor. Freund noted that 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 had not yet been widely integrated, and mostly only in pre-release versions.

The lessons: compare release archives with the tagged git tree; build from git where you can; treat opaque binary files as code; and investigate performance regressions in security-critical paths.

blocks.code:
# Am I running a backdoored version? (5.6.0 and 5.6.1)
xz --version

# Does sshd load liblzma on this host? (via libsystemd on patched distros)
ldd /usr/sbin/sshd | grep -E 'liblzma|libsystemd'

# Compare a release tarball with the tagged git tree
tar xf xz-5.6.1.tar.gz
git clone https://git.tukaani.org/xz.git xz-git && git -C xz-git checkout -q v5.6.1
diff -rq xz-5.6.1 xz-git | grep -v '\.git'   # expect generated files; read every one
blocks.caption: Defender checks. The diff is noisy because tarballs legitimately contain generated Autotools files, which is exactly why the malicious m4 line blended in. Each extra file deserves a look.

blocks.question: Why did reviewing the xz git repository not reveal the backdoor's trigger?
options: The trigger line in build-to-host.m4 existed only in the release tarballs, not in git
The repository was encrypted
Git history was rewritten to remove it
Reviewers only read C files
blocks.explain: Freund: that line is not in the upstream source of build-to-host, nor is build-to-host used by xz in git, but it is present in the release tarballs. The payload in git looked like test data.

blocks.question: Which distribution practice would have kept the backdoor out of a package even if the 5.6.1 version was adopted?
options: Verifying the maintainer's signature on the tarball
Running the package's test suite
Using a newer compiler
Building the package from the tagged git source instead of the release tarball
blocks.explain: The trigger lived only in the tarball. Arch Linux switched xz to build from git when the backdoor was disclosed. The signature was valid (Jia Tan signed it), and the tests passed.

lessons.title: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook

blocks.md:
Sooner or later an advisory will name something you use. The first hours decide how bad it gets. The playbook below is assembled from the guidance published in this course's cases: CISA's tj-actions alert, the axios post-mortem, GitHub's ua-parser-js advisory and Codecov's notice.

The key mindset: a malicious package is not a bug to patch. It ran code with the rights of whatever installed it. Treat it as an intrusion. GitHub's ua-parser-js advisory: any computer with the package installed or running should be considered fully compromised, and all secrets and keys on it rotated immediately **from a different computer**.

blocks.title: Response playbook for a compromised dependency

scenes.caption: 1. Scope: which versions, which time window? (axios: 1.14.1 and 0.30.4, 00:21 to 03:15 UTC on 31 March 2026.) Then search lockfiles, SBOMs, caches and CI logs.
2. Contain: block the versions in your registry proxy, pin or override to a known-good version, and stop pipelines that would reinstall the bad one.
3. Assume compromise of every machine that installed or ran it in the window: developer laptops, CI runners, build images, servers.
4. Rotate every secret those machines could read, from a clean machine: cloud keys, registry and GitHub tokens, SSH keys, signing keys.
5. Hunt: network logs for published indicators (domains, IPs), unexpected processes or persistence, and use of rotated credentials before rotation.
6. Rebuild affected hosts and artifacts from clean sources, then report to the registry, the project and (if required) authorities, and fix the gap that let it in.

blocks.code:
# Scope: the axios post-mortem's grep (suits pnpm-style lockfiles; the next line covers package-lock.json)
grep -E " axios@(1\.14\.1|0\.30\.4)|plain-crypto-js " package-lock.json yarn.lock 2>/dev/null
grep -rE '"(node_modules/)?plain-crypto-js"' --include=package-lock.json .

# Scope: which repositories in the org use a compromised action?
gh search code "tj-actions/changed-files" --owner my-org --filename "*.yml"

# Scope: which workflow runs happened inside the exposure window?
gh run list --workflow ci.yml --created "2025-03-12..2025-03-15" \
  --json databaseId,createdAt,headBranch

# Contain: force a known-good version everywhere in the tree
npm pkg set overrides.axios=1.14.0 && npm install
blocks.caption: Real commands. For CI compromises, CISA's tj-actions steps were: identify repositories and runs in the window, check logs for exposed secrets (possibly double base64-encoded), rotate them all, and pin to a safe commit.

blocks.md:
**Things responders get wrong.**

- **Upgrading and stopping there.** Removing the package does not remove what it installed. The axios dropper fetched a separate remote access trojan; GitHub's advisory noted there is no guarantee that removing the package removes all malicious software.
- **Rotating from the infected machine.** The attacker watches the new secret being typed. Rotate from a clean device.
- **Forgetting CI and caches.** Runner caches, Docker layers and artifact proxies can keep serving the bad tarball after the registry removes it; CISA's Shai-Hulud guidance says to search cached versions in artifact repositories.
- **Missing the transitive path.** Search lockfiles, not package.json: plain-crypto-js never appeared in anyone's package.json.

Then close the gap that let it in: lockfile plus `npm ci`, install scripts blocked, a release-age cooldown, actions pinned to SHAs, secrets moved to short-lived OIDC credentials, and an SBOM inventory so the next scoping step takes minutes.

Malicious dependency equals intrusion. Scope by version and time window, contain, assume every machine that ran it is compromised, rotate secrets from a clean machine, hunt, rebuild, then fix the control that failed.

blocks.question: A developer's laptop installed axios 1.14.1 at 01:10 UTC on 31 March 2026. They have since upgraded to 1.15.0. What is the correct next step?
options: Nothing: the upgrade removed the malicious code
Treat the laptop as compromised: rotate every credential it held from another machine, investigate it, and rebuild it
Run npm audit and close the ticket if it is clean
Delete node_modules and reinstall
blocks.explain: The postinstall dropper installed a separate remote access trojan and erased its traces. The axios post-mortem says to treat the machine as compromised and rotate every secret, token and credential on it.

blocks.question: After the tj-actions compromise, a public repository finds the action ran during the window. Why is rotating secrets urgent even though no data went to an attacker's server?
options: Because the malicious code also deleted the repository
Because GitHub automatically shares secrets with forks
Because the secrets were printed, encoded, into workflow logs that anyone can read in a public repository
It is not urgent; encoding protects them
blocks.explain: The payload dumped runner memory into the job log, double base64-encoded, which is trivially reversible. Public repository logs are public, so every secret in that run must be considered exposed.

blocks.md: **Practise legally.** OWASP Juice Shop, a deliberately insecure web shop you run locally, has Vulnerable Components challenges including two typosquatting challenges and a supply chain attack challenge ([companion guide](https://pwning.owasp-juice.shop/companion-guide/latest/part2/vulnerable-components.html)). On your own repositories: run [OpenSSF Scorecard](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard), pin your GitHub Actions to SHAs, generate an SBOM with `npm sbom`, and point the OSV script from lesson 15 at your lockfiles. GitHub Security Lab's [resources](https://securitylab.github.com/) include the workflow-security series used in lesson 10. Only test systems and accounts you own or have written permission to test.
